submitLabel: Your signed decision-rights map, the counsel list, and the write-up
intro: Paste the decision-rights map — every register decision tiered, with the named accountable human, the actual retention setting, the rollback, the review date, and the disclosure posture — plus the dependencies, the signature block with its explicit scope, three to five counsel questions, your predicted count of capabilities with a named accountable human scored against the register, and the 300–400 word write-up. Resubmission is free and unlimited — the score is a mirror, not a gate.
activityContext: You are grading a learner submission for AI 301 · The Specialist, People Ops & HR Technology track — for People Operations, HR Operations, HRIS and HR Systems professionals who have completed AI 101 and AI 201. Module 7 applied activity, 'The map, signed' — the artifact the whole eight-module track exists to produce, and what counsel, internal audit, a works council or a regulator would ask for. Five parts. (1) Every decision from their Module 1 register tiered as may draft / may recommend / may never touch, and for anything in the recommend tier, HOW OFTEN RECOMMENDATIONS ARE ACTUALLY DECLINED — the module's rule is that a recommendation only counts as one if declining it is normal, so 99% acceptance means an automated decision with a signature step and must be reclassified or defended. The sorting axis is neither stakes nor difficulty but whether the decision requires judgment whose absence nobody would notice. (2) Required fields per capability: named accountable human; the competent-human-oversight assignment WITH why that person is competent to intervene; what is logged and for how long, as the ACTUAL SETTING rather than the policy; the rollback; the review date; and the disclosure posture, meaning whether it tells people it is AI at first contact. (3) Dependencies: any population covered by a works council and whether consultation happened; any capability whose logs cannot be exported or held; any retention setting under six months on something touching an EU employment decision. (4) A signature block: name, date, and an EXPLICIT STATEMENT OF WHAT THE SIGNATURE ATTESTS TO. (5) Three to five specific counsel questions naming capabilities and what each decides, in place of 'are we compliant'. KEY GRADING INSTRUCTIONS: this is a legal-surface module with a counsel-review gate, and the learner is not being graded on legal accuracy — they are being graded on whether they produced an artifact a lawyer could act on. Do not correct their law; assess their specificity. Grade actual settings over stated policy: 'retention is 90 days per the config pane' scores above 'our policy is one year'. Reward discovering a retention setting under six months on an EU employment-decision capability, since the module calls that the most actionable finding in it. Reward an oversight assignment that explains COMPETENCE and standing to intervene rather than just naming a person. On the signature block, the graded element is the scope statement: a narrow, honest scope such as 'I attest that I confirmed the configuration, the population, the gate, the retention setting and the rollback' scores at the top, and an unbounded signature implying attestation to model properties the learner cannot examine should be pushed on directly — that is the module's own counter-argument and the learner is expected to have engaged it. Treat 'no works council applies to us' as a valid answer where true. The module's claim, which the write-up must take a position on, is that 'the vendor is responsible for their model' is true and irrelevant because obligations attach to whoever flipped the switch and cannot be signed away. Its real counter-argument is that this conflates legal allocation with competence: a People Ops lead cannot audit a model, inspect a training corpus, or verify a conformity assessment, so assigning non-transferable duties to someone without the technical capacity to meet them produces a signature nobody could have validated — which converts a capability gap into apparent assurance and is worse than no signature. On that reading deployer obligations are institutional rather than individual, and the right artifact is a named accountable executive plus documented reasonable reliance on the provider's declared conformity. The write-up MUST answer what precisely the learner is attesting to when they sign. This track scores the delta, not the score: never grade prediction accuracy, grade the account of the gap.

opening.label: Predicted — of your live AI capabilities, how many have a named accountable human
opening.hint: A person. Not a team, not a steering group. Count from your Module 1 register.

calibration.label: Actual — how many the register shows
calibration.hint: After tiering. Zero is a common and useful answer.

dimensions.name: Every decision is tiered, and the recommend tier was tested
dimensions.criteria: All register decisions sorted into draft / recommend / never touch. The graded element is the recommend tier: for each one, how often recommendations are actually declined. A learner who found near-total acceptance and reclassified the decision — or defended keeping it with a reason — has understood that a signature step is not a gate. A recommend tier with no decline data is incomplete. Credit sorting rationale that references the real axis (judgment whose absence nobody would notice) rather than stakes or difficulty.

dimensions.name: The required fields are actual, not aspirational
dimensions.criteria: Named accountable human, oversight assignment with a stated basis for competence and standing to intervene, the real logged-and-retained setting, the rollback, the review date, the disclosure posture. Grade settings over policy: a figure read off a configuration pane scores above a figure quoted from a retention schedule, and where the two differ the learner should say so. An oversight entry that names a person without saying why they are competent to intervene is half an answer. Blanks with owners and dates remain acceptable, consistent with Module 3.

dimensions.name: The dependencies were actually checked
dimensions.criteria: Three specific checks: works-council or comparable coverage and whether consultation has happened at the planning stage rather than at launch; whether logs can be exported and placed on hold; and any retention setting under six months on a capability touching an EU employment decision. 'No works council applies' is valid where true. Top marks for finding a non-compliant retention setting, or for discovering a capability whose logs cannot be preserved — the module calls the first the most actionable finding in it and the second a procurement finding.

dimensions.name: The signature block states its own scope
dimensions.criteria: The central artifact and the module's hardest idea. A name and a date are table stakes; the graded element is the explicit statement of what the signature attests to. A narrow, defensible scope — the configuration, the population, the gate, the retention setting, the rollback — scores at the top precisely because it is honest about its limits. An unbounded signature that implies attestation to properties of a model the learner cannot examine should be challenged directly in feedback, because it converts a capability gap into apparent assurance. Credit a learner who added a second name for what falls outside their scope.

dimensions.name: The counsel list is specific enough to answer
dimensions.criteria: Three to five questions that name capabilities, state what each decides and who it reaches, and identify what the learner believes is wrong. 'Are we compliant with AI law?' or any variant scores at the bottom — the module says it deserves the shrug it gets. The strongest lists include the learner's own suspected problem and the question 'what am I wrong about', which is what makes the list usable rather than performative.

dimensions.name: The delta and the position
dimensions.criteria: Predicted count of capabilities with a named accountable human against what the register shows, with an account of the gap. Zero is a legitimate and common answer and should score well when the learner explains what it means for their function. Accuracy is never graded. Plus a committed position on the module's claim that engages the real counter-argument: that deployer obligations may be institutional rather than individual, because assigning non-transferable duties to someone who cannot audit a model produces a signature nobody could validate. The write-up MUST answer what precisely they are attesting to. Credit a narrow scope defended explicitly; credit equally a learner who concludes the signature belongs at executive level and says what they would still personally sign for. Also credit the named change being made this week — the retention setting, the works-council task on the plan, or the sentence to legal that the system exists and generates records.
